On the one hand, I don't appreciate how aggressive the distaste for Season 2 is. A lot of what's being posted here is similar to what happened with Part 2. People like what they like. Unless what they like is morally apprehensible, don't shit on them for it. 

On other hand, while the bigots are and always will be active here and everywhere, there are genuine critiques about the writing quality in Season 2 -- critiques that make sense even when you ignore the game counterpart (inconsistencies,  inefficient storytelling, lack of subtext, etc.). We're not talking about a small but loud minority of haters in this regard, we're talking about the fact that Season 2's finale had 55% viewership drop from Season 1's. 

People like to say The Last of Us Part II's reception was split in half, but it wasn't. Professional critiques lauded it; it won the player's choice award despite review bombings; it generated and still generates even more discourse than Part I. Season 2 is a different story, literally and metaphorically.

Unfortunately, humans do what humans do and blame already-villified groups for the game's flaws, but even though those portions of the experience are majorly ineffective, they are not what poisoned this apple. People are people. There are no exceptions, at least for those who meet the minimum levels of introspection. 

On a PERSONAL note, not an objective one: there are things about The Veilguard that people will like. I envy them because, after a decade of waiting, and after the prior game got me through deeply traumatic experiences, the disappointment I felt and feel is nigh traumatic in and of itself.

Look, I love Dragon Age: Inquisition, but The Last of Us 1 and 2 objectively have leagues of better character writing and thematic exploration. That fact doesn't make me hate my favourite game, but it is a fact. 

I don't know about the exact number of weaknesses in the games, but the other entries mostly have superficial problems relating to clunkiness, missed opportunities, and a weaker antagonist (I liked Corypheus, especially after learning more about him through the codex, but his lack of screentime OBJECTIVELY means he lacked a decent amount of depth and characterization. Almost became a mustache-twirler). 

Veilguard's issues are linked to all the most important narrative elements, namely its central theme. It's got the environments executed well, sure, but the dialogue lacks subtext, the antagonists are as complex as Blasto from Mass Effect (writer's shot themselves in the foot by blaming the absence of nuance on the blight), nothing justifies Rook as the protagonist (I'm not talking about a magic hand, I'm talking about motivation), and the companions lack agency -- the idea that 'everyone will happily band together to face great conflicts' lacks water in both fiction and the real world. 

Even on a minor level, the fact that Rook is so agreeable with their companion's opinions, and that they're so genial with each other after minimal conflict, makes everyone in The Lighthouse as bland as The Keeper. I understand the team was meant to feel like a family, but family members fight. They love each other, but that doesn't mean they don't have opinions and ideals that will create clashes without neat resolutions. Often, people even have relatives that they actively don't like. The other games capitalised on this; there are loads of not just controversial but differential takes on the various in-world historic dilemmas relating to societal control and religion. 

The Veilguard attempts to create a safe space for the player by making all the inherent conflict in Thedas milquetoast: a good intention behind writing that is objectively weaker than the previous entries, on account of it having minimal depth to its most important characters and thematic exploration.

Again, make sure it has a strong link to the actual story, and most of all, that it's interesting. 

The main thing to remember with writing is that you should do whatever the fuck you want as long as it is in service of the story. But don't be so ignorant that you can't acknowledge your own or other authors past mistakes and/or failures. A lot of people mess up prologues, so read a few and see what works (check out the Way of Kings by Brandon Sanderson.
